title: AP Physics 1: Algebra-Based
summary: Practise motion, force, energy, momentum, rotation, oscillations and fluids.
frameworkNote: Unit map checked against College Board on 15 October 2026 for the 2026-27 course. Each unit has one focused original revision lesson, not exhaustive topic coverage or an official practice paper. Uses the current eight-unit framework, including fluids in Unit 8. These models do not replace experimental investigations.

modules.title: Position, velocity and constant acceleration
modules.focus: Read a motion model with a chosen positive direction.
explanation: Displacement is final position minus initial position; distance counts the total path length. Average velocity divides displacement by elapsed time. Choose a positive direction before assigning signs so that opposite motion is represented consistently.

For constant acceleration, v=v₀+at and Δx=v₀t+at²/2. These equations are not valid with a changing acceleration unless applied in intervals where the assumption holds. On a velocity-time graph, signed area gives displacement.

workedExample.prompt: A cart starts at 2 m/s and accelerates uniformly at 3 m/s² for 4 s. Find velocity and displacement.

misconception.claim: Negative velocity always means negative acceleration.
misconception.correction: Velocity gives direction of motion; acceleration gives change of velocity.

questions.prompt: A runner moves 30 m east then 10 m west in 10 s. Find average velocity east-positive.
An object at rest accelerates at 2 m/s² for 3 s. Find displacement.

modules.title: Free-body diagrams and net force
modules.focus: Sum interactions acting on one chosen object.
explanation: A free-body diagram includes forces exerted on the selected object, not the forces it exerts on other objects. Newton’s second law relates the vector sum of those forces to ma. Zero net force means constant velocity, which can be nonzero.

Newton’s third-law partners act on different objects and therefore do not cancel within one object’s force sum. Circular motion requires inward net force; it is provided by physical interactions such as tension or gravity, not an additional force called centripetal force.

workedExample.prompt: A 4 kg cart experiences 18 N right and 6 N left. Find acceleration.
steps: Choose right-positive and sum forces: 18-6=12 N.

misconception.claim: Third-law force pairs cancel on the same free-body diagram.

questions.prompt: A 2 kg mass moves in a circle of radius 3 m at 6 m/s. Find inward net force.
A book rests on a table. Are its weight and normal force a third-law pair?
questions.hint: Identify the object each force acts on.
questions.answer: No. Both act on the book; their third-law partners act on Earth and the table.
checkpoints: Pair forces across two interacting objects.
Distinguish equilibrium from a third-law pair.

modules.title: Work and kinetic energy
explanation: For a constant force, work is Fd cos θ, where θ is the angle between force and displacement. Net work changes kinetic energy. A force perpendicular to motion does no work even though it can change the direction of velocity.

Energy conservation is applied to a defined system. Friction may convert mechanical energy to thermal energy rather than destroy total energy. Power measures the rate of energy transfer and is expressed in watts, equivalent to joules per second.

workedExample.prompt: A 2 kg cart initially at rest receives 16 J of net work. Find final speed.

misconception.claim: Energy lost from motion has disappeared.
misconception.correction: It may have transferred to thermal, sound or other energy within a larger system.

questions.prompt: A 10 N force parallel to motion acts over 3 m. Find work.
A device transfers 600 J in 4 s. Find average power.

modules.title: Impulse and a sticking collision
modules.focus: Conserve momentum only for an appropriate system.
explanation: Momentum is mass times velocity and is a vector. Impulse equals the change in momentum and is the signed area under a force-time graph. A small average force acting longer can produce the same impulse as a larger force acting briefly.

Total momentum is conserved when the external impulse on the selected system is negligible. In a sticking collision, kinetic energy usually decreases even though system momentum is conserved. Include both colliding objects and retain velocity directions.

workedExample.prompt: A 2 kg cart moving at 3 m/s sticks to a stationary 1 kg cart. Find their common speed.
steps: The combined mass is 3 kg, so final velocity is 6/3=2 m/s in the initial direction.

misconception.claim: Momentum conservation means kinetic energy is always conserved.
misconception.correction: Kinetic energy can be converted internally in an inelastic collision.

questions.prompt: A 0.5 kg ball changes velocity from +4 to -2 m/s. Find impulse.
A constant 12 N net force acts for 0.25 s. Find momentum change.
questions.answer: 3 kg m/s in the force direction.
checkpoints: Recognise N s equals kg m/s.

modules.title: Torque and angular acceleration
modules.focus: Measure force effectiveness about an axis.
explanation: Torque magnitude is rF sin θ, using the angle between the position vector from the axis and the force. A force through the axis has zero lever arm. Specify an axis and a positive rotation direction before adding torques.

For fixed-axis rotation with constant moment of inertia, net torque equals Iα. Moment of inertia depends on mass distribution as well as total mass. Moving the same mass farther from an axis increases its contribution mr².

workedExample.prompt: A perpendicular 8 N force acts 0.5 m from an axle. If I=2 kg m², find angular acceleration.

misconception.claim: Torque depends only on force magnitude.
misconception.correction: Distance from the axis and force direction also matter.

questions.prompt: A 10 N force acts along a line through the rotation axis. Find torque.
checkpoints: A large force can still have zero torque.

questions.prompt: A point mass moves from radius r to 2r about the same axis. How does its inertia change?
questions.answer: It becomes four times as large.

modules.title: Angular momentum and rolling energy
explanation: Angular momentum about a fixed axis is Iω for a rigid body in that rotation model. It is conserved when net external torque about the chosen axis is zero. Changing I can therefore change ω without an external torque.

Rolling without slipping combines centre-of-mass translation with rotation and satisfies v=ωR. Total kinetic energy is mv²/2+Iω²/2. Rotational energy must be included when relating a rolling object’s height loss to its speed.

workedExample.prompt: A rotating student reduces moment of inertia from 4 to 2 kg m² while external torque is negligible. Initial angular speed is 3 rad/s. Find final speed.
steps: Initial angular momentum is 4(3)=12 kg m²/s.

misconception.claim: Conserving angular momentum always conserves rotational kinetic energy.
misconception.correction: Internal work can change kinetic energy while angular momentum stays constant.

questions.prompt: A wheel rolls without slipping at 6 m/s with radius 0.3 m. Find ω.
For I=2 kg m² and ω=4 rad/s, find rotational kinetic energy.

modules.title: Spring oscillations and restoring force
explanation: An ideal horizontal spring-mass oscillator obeys F=-kx about equilibrium. The minus sign means force opposes displacement, not necessarily velocity. For mass m, angular frequency is √(k/m) and period is 2π√(m/k).

Total mechanical energy is kA²/2 in the ideal undamped model. Speed is greatest at equilibrium, while spring potential energy is greatest at the turning points. Increasing amplitude changes energy but not the period of this ideal linear oscillator.

workedExample.prompt: A 1 kg mass on a 16 N/m spring oscillates ideally. Find angular frequency and period.

misconception.claim: The restoring force is largest at equilibrium.
misconception.correction: Spring displacement and restoring force are zero there; speed is largest.

questions.prompt: If mass quadruples with the same spring constant, how does period change?
For k=100 N/m and amplitude 0.20 m, find total oscillator energy.

modules.title: Pressure, buoyancy and fluid continuity
modules.focus: Use depth and displaced volume with clear assumptions.
explanation: In a stationary fluid of uniform density, pressure increases with depth by ρgh. Pressure is force per area; it is not itself a force. The buoyant force equals the weight of displaced fluid, not automatically the weight of the object.

For steady incompressible flow through a full pipe, A₁v₁=A₂v₂. A narrower section therefore has greater flow speed when volumetric flow is unchanged. Bernoulli’s relation additionally assumes a suitable streamline and negligible viscous losses.

workedExample.prompt: A fully submerged object displaces 0.003 m³ of water. Use ρ=1,000 kg/m³ and g=10 m/s². Find buoyant force.
steps: Displaced water mass is ρV=3 kg.
Its weight, and hence buoyant force, is 30 N upward.

misconception.claim: Every submerged object has buoyant force equal to its own weight.
misconception.correction: Equality occurs in vertical force balance; displaced fluid determines buoyancy.

questions.prompt: Find gauge pressure 2 m below water’s surface using ρ=1,000 and g=10 in SI units.
A pipe’s area halves in steady incompressible flow. What happens to speed?
